clinicalPearls: Uncommon stones composed of ammonium acid urate, whose formation requires both a high urinary ammonium and a high urate

There are two classic settings: chronic laxative abuse and eating disorders in the developed world, and endemic bladder stones from childhood malnutrition and low-phosphate diets in the developing world
Chronic diarrhoea or laxative misuse causes volume depletion, a low urine volume, acidic urine and potassium depletion that increases renal ammonium production
Recurrent urinary infection and dehydration are contributing factors
Stones are radiolucent to only faintly opaque, so non-contrast CT is the best imaging modality
Their presence should prompt sensitive enquiry into laxative misuse or an eating disorder, which is often concealed
Management targets the cause, namely stopping laxative abuse, rehydration, correcting hypokalaemia and treating any infection, alongside stone removal
Because they are hard, ammonium acid urate stones respond poorly to shock-wave lithotripsy and often need endoscopic or percutaneous removal
reference.pathophysiology: Ammonium acid urate precipitates when the urine contains both abundant urate and a high concentration of ammonium. This occurs when chronic diarrhoea or laxative misuse produces volume depletion and a metabolic acidosis with potassium depletion: the low urine volume concentrates solutes, the acidic pH favours the urate species, and hypokalaemia together with intestinal alkali loss stimulates renal ammoniagenesis, supplying the ammonium. Recurrent infection and dehydration reinforce the process. In malnourished children on low-phosphate, low-protein diets, high urinary urate and ammonium similarly drive endemic bladder stone formation.
additionalInvestigations: Non-contrast CT, since these stones are poorly seen on plain films
Stone analysis identifying ammonium acid urate
24-hour urine for volume, urate, pH and ammonium
Serum electrolytes for hypokalaemia and metabolic acidosis
Sensitive assessment for laxative misuse or an eating disorder
redFlags: Severe electrolyte disturbance from laxative abuse, such as hypokalaemia and acidosis
Features of a serious underlying eating disorder
Recurrent stones despite apparent treatment, suggesting ongoing concealed misuse
reference.prognosis: Correcting the underlying cause by stopping laxative misuse, rehydrating and restoring electrolytes prevents recurrence; persistent concealed misuse leads to recurrent stones and ongoing metabolic disturbance.
pitfalls: Failing to ask sensitively about laxative misuse or an eating disorder
Relying on plain radiographs, which miss these radiolucent stones
Expecting shock-wave lithotripsy to work on these hard stones
Overlooking hypokalaemia and metabolic acidosis that need correction
management: Correct the underlying cause by stopping laxative misuse, treating any eating disorder and addressing childhood malnutrition and low-phosphate diet
Maintain high fluid intake and rehydration to raise urine volume and reduce solute concentration
Restore potassium and correct the metabolic acidosis, which reduces renal ammonium production
Remove existing stones by endourological means such as ureteroscopy or percutaneous nephrolithotomy, since these poorly opaque stones respond poorly to shock-wave lithotripsy
Reduce urinary urate with dietary purine moderation and, where appropriate, urate-lowering therapy such as allopurinol
Provide sensitive psychiatric and dietetic support for concealed laxative misuse or an eating disorder
Monitor with periodic imaging and metabolic urine studies to prevent recurrence
